issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger profile mixes tactile/startle-type cues and driving-with-others cues that could fit war-zone trauma, but 'being looked at sexually' points toward a sexual-threat trauma context that is not supported elsewhere in memory, threat, or appraisal items. This specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The dominant threat items describe generalized vigilance and fear of interpersonal attack. In combination with the sexual-objectification trigger, this pulls the profile toward an interpersonal/sexual trauma formulation, whereas the memory and appraisal items do not contain corresponding themes. This creates cross-node incoherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear link to the other selected items. The rest of the appraisals center on unfairness, shame, and inability to trust oneself; without any role-related trauma content in memory, triggers, or threat, this item feels weakly anchored and clinically mismatched relative to the otherwise war-zone/interpersonal-danger presentation.

vignette: Kiri had been twenty-two when the convoy broke apart. She remembered the road tearing upward in a single, blinding arc, followed by a sound that emptied the air from her lungs. Before she could stand, rough hands seized her upper arms, hauling her into the dirt. She was a civilian caught in the crossfire of a neighborhood she had no part in, watching strangers fall as the sky repeatedly cracked open. The chaos of that afternoon did not stay in the past. It settled into the rhythm of her breathing and the way her eyes moved. When the fighting ended and she was finally evacuated, Kiri returned to her veterinary clinic in the Pacific Northwest, expecting to resume her work treating animals and consulting with clients. Instead, she found herself bracing for the next impact. The clinic became a landscape of quiet alarms. She could not relax in her office, even with the heavy door closed and the street outside still. Her eyes never stopped moving, tracking the parking lot, the street, the door hinges, cataloging every shift in light and sound. At work, she kept her posture rigid, waiting for the shift that would demand she step outside. The sounds of her environment—the backfire of a passing truck, the sudden thud of a supply crate—made her shoulders lock. What frightened her most was the sudden contact of an unexpected touch. She had come to believe that any hand reaching for her without warning carried the weight of that dirt road. When a fellow vet tech tapped her shoulder to hand her a chart, Kiri flinched so violently she dropped her pen, her heart hammering against her ribs as if the pavement were rising to meet her again. She began asking clients and staff to call out before approaching her. Her husband noticed how her posture changed the moment they shared a car. They had been driving together less often since the memories tightened their grip. When he offered to take the wheel so she could rest, she found herself unable to sit beside him in the front seat. The sensation of being alongside someone while moving at speed felt like surrendering control. She started taking the long route to the clinic alone, leaving her house twenty minutes early to avoid the morning commute, telling her husband she needed the quiet. The habit solidified over months. She avoided the passenger seat entirely, even when he asked her to sit beside him in the theater or at a family gathering, because the shared space and the sudden proximity of strangers felt like a trap. She was certain that if she allowed herself to lean back, the ground would drop away. Nights were the hardest. She lay awake because she needed to stay alert, certain that sleep would make her vulnerable to another ambush. Her mind offered no quiet, only the same sequence of events playing over and over, unedited and relentless. The images did not arrive as a story. They came in fragmented pieces that did not fit together: a boot on gravel, a child’s shoe on the roadside, the smell of burnt rubber, a voice shouting directions she could not understand. When the pieces surfaced, shame flooded her chest. She felt intense shame on recall, convinced that she should have anticipated the collapse, that she should have known how to move, that her own instincts had failed her. She could not rely on herself to predict what would happen next. What stayed with her was the certainty that bad things happen without warning and nothing has been done about it. The injustice of it sat heavy in her stomach, a quiet anger that mirrored her helplessness. By the time she scheduled an intake, Kiri had spent years building a life around anticipation. She had learned to sit with her back against the wall at every restaurant, to keep her keys in her right hand, to measure the distance between herself and every door. The weight of it finally outweighed the fear of being examined. She was hoping for a way to stop scanning every room and a way to quiet the film in her head. What she feared most was that the damage was permanent, that she would never again trust the floor beneath her or the people sitting next to her. She wanted to know if she could ever let herself sleep without counting the seconds, and if there was a way to feel safe in a world that had already proven it could take everything away.
